runs.text: No paradigm always wins: each one makes one kind of change easy.
The kiosk is going to receive three change requests: adding a
. The till is written in three ways: with orders that change boxes, with pieces that keep their state and with calculations that change nothing.
Choose by eye, before looking at the code, which version you would change with the least effort for each request.

The tax is a new operation on the same data: the functional version adds it with a function. The payment method is a new kind of thing that meets a contract: the object version adds it with a class. The report is another transformation of the sales: again, the functional one. The imperative one works while the program is short.
A paradigm is a way of organising a program; in imperative programming, the program is a list of orders that change memory.

entries.text: What goes in and what comes out?
The same in all three versions: the test order, 3 juices and 2 sandwiches, and its total.
Which part is calculation and which part touches the world?
The total and the discount are calculation; showing them touches the world.

runs.text: The paradigm is chosen by the kind of change expected, not by taste
A real program usually mixes them: a functional core for the calculations, objects for what has state, such as the inventory, and a short imperative edge that reads and shows.

points.text: Objects make it easy to add new kinds of things that share a contract.
Functions make it easy to add new operations on the same data.
The imperative style is direct for short programs that do one thing.

entries.text: The three paradigms are decades old; what matters is which change each one makes easy.
Ask them to name the change they expect before choosing.
